title: Acclimatisation: minutes, days, weeks
goal: Describe what the body changes in the first minutes, days and weeks at altitude, what is still disputed, and how mountain sickness is avoided.

steps.title: Minutes: breathe more, heart faster
steps.text:
The first response takes minutes. Sensors in the neck arteries ([peripheral chemoreceptors](g:peripheral-chemoreceptor)) notice the low oxygen pressure and drive [minute ventilation](g:minute-ventilation) up: the [hypoxic ventilatory response](g:hypoxic-ventilatory-response). Heart rate rises too, and [stroke volume](g:stroke-volume) falls very little [[c:acc-acute]].

Extra breathing blows off CO₂, which makes the blood too alkaline ([respiratory alkalosis](g:respiratory-alkalosis)). Over the next days the kidneys correct that, and breathing can rise further. All these adjustments together are [altitude acclimatisation](g:altitude-acclimatisation), the same idea as the heat version you met earlier: a few days for the fast changes, weeks for the slow ones.

claims.text: In acute exposure to altitude, ventilation and heart rate rise with a minimal fall in stroke volume.

evidence.quote: In acute exposure, ventilation and heart rate are elevated with a minimum reduction in stroke volume.

steps.title: Hours: EPO. Weeks: red cells
steps.text:
The signal for new red cells starts fast. In six volunteers at a simulated 3,000 m, [EPO](g:epo) was already raised after 114 minutes and kept rising; the calculated production rate was 1.8 times higher at 3,000 m and 3.0 times higher at 4,000 m [[c:acc-epo-fast]].

But [red cell production](g:red-cell-production) (erythropoiesis) is slow: new cells take days to appear and weeks to add up. In a trial of 39 runners, 4 weeks at 2,500 m raised red cell mass by 9% and VO₂max by 5% [[c:acc-rcm-weeks]]. The EPO rise can fade while you stay: in runners at 1,780 m it was back to baseline after 72 h [[c:acc-epo-fade]].

claims.text: EPO rises within about 2 hours of simulated altitude, with production rising about 1.8 times at 3,000 m and 3.0 times at 4,000 m.

evidence.quote: EPO levels during hypoxia were significantly elevated after 114 and 84 min (3,000 and 4,000 m), rising thereafter continuously for the period investigated.
This rise in EPO levels corresponds to 1.8-fold (3,000 m) and 3.0-fold (4,000 m) increases in the calculated production rate of the hormone.

claims.text: In runners living at 1,780 m, EPO was raised at 24 and 48 h but back to sea-level baseline after 72 h.

evidence.quote: EPO was significantly higher in all groups at 24 and 48 h, but returned to sea level baseline after 72 h in the 1,780-m group.

claims.text: Four weeks of living at 2,500 m raised red cell mass by about 9% and VO₂max by about 5% in runners.

evidence.quote: Both altitude groups significantly increased VO2 max (5%) in direct proportion to an increase in red cell mass volume (9%; r = 0.37, P < 0.05), neither of which changed in the control.

In addition, plasma volume is reduced over 24-48 h to improve the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, and is further improved during a prolonged sojourn at altitude through an enhanced erythropoiesis and larger Hb mass, allowing for a partial or full restoration of the blood volume and arterial oxygen content.

steps.title: Days: plasma shrinks first
steps.text:
Within 24–48 h [plasma volume](g:plasma-volume) falls [[c:acc-pv-fall]]. Red cells are not added yet, but the same haemoglobin sits in less fluid, so the concentration of haemoglobin rises and each litre of blood carries more oxygen. In 8 elite cyclists at 2,340 m, haemoglobin concentration and arterial O₂ content rose during acclimatisation [[c:acc-hb-conc]].

So an early rise in haemoglobin *concentration* is not a rise in haemoglobin *mass*. Blood volume = plasma + red cells; concentration = Hb mass ÷ blood volume.

claims.text: Plasma volume falls over the first 24–48 h at altitude, raising the oxygen-carrying capacity of each litre of blood.

evidence.quote: In addition, plasma volume is reduced over 24-48 h to improve the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, and is further improved during a prolonged sojourn at altitude through an enhanced erythropoiesis and larger Hb mass, allowing for a partial or full restoration of the blood volume and arterial oxygen content.

claims.text: In elite cyclists at 2,340 m, acclimatisation raised haemoglobin concentration and arterial O₂ content.

evidence.quote: Acclimatization increased hemoglobin concentration and arterial oxygen content.

steps.title: Haemoglobin concentration after plasma loss
steps.problem: A man has 800 g of haemoglobin in 5.0 L of blood (3.0 L plasma, 2.0 L red cells): 160 g·L⁻¹. His plasma volume falls 10% and his haemoglobin mass is unchanged. What is the new concentration?
steps: Plasma falls 10%: 3.0 × 0.90 = 2.7 L. Red cells stay at 2.0 L.
Concentration = 800 ÷ 4.7 = 170 g·L⁻¹, up 6%, with no new red cells. A 10% plasma loss gives a 6% rise, not 10%, because plasma is only part of the blood.

steps.title: Weeks: does VO₂max come back?
steps.text: After 4 or more weeks the blood's oxygen content is back to normal. A review of the field adds that at higher altitudes maximal heart rate and so peak cardiac output also fall [[c:acc-plateau-claim]]. The sources disagree on what that means for VO₂max measured at altitude.

claims.text: After 4 or more weeks above about 2,000 m, arterial O₂ content is normalised; whether VO₂max at altitude recovers is disputed (essentially unchanged in a review, up about 8% from the day-1 value in 14 days in one study).

evidence.quote: At these higher altitudes additional adaptations occur, one being a reduction in the maximal heart rate response and consequently a lower peak cardiac output.

Thus, in spite of a normalization of the arterial oxygen content after 4 or more weeks at altitude, the peak oxygen uptake reached after a long acclimatization period is essentially unaltered compared with acute exposure.

Subsequently, these parameters increased by 3.2% (P<0.05) and 6.0% (P<0.05) from Days 1 to 7, by 4.8% (P<0.05) and 5.7% (P<0.05) from Days 7 to 14, followed by 0.7% (P>0.05) and 1.4% (P>0.05) from Days 14 to 21, respectively.

debate.question: Does acclimatisation win back VO₂max measured at altitude?

sides.position: Partly: elite cyclists at 2,340 m raised VO₂max about 8% above their day-1 value in 14 days (+3.2% by day 7, +4.8% more by day 14), still about 5–6% below sea level, then little more.
No: after a long stay, peak VO₂ at altitude is essentially the same as on arrival, because lower peak heart rate and cardiac output offset the better blood oxygen content.

steps.title: The cost: mountain sickness
steps.text:
[Acute mountain sickness](g:acute-mountain-sickness) (AMS) is headache with nausea and loss of appetite. It is mild and temporary in 10–30% of people at 2,500–3,000 m [[c:acc-ams-prev]]. Lung fluid ([HAPE](g:hape)) is rare below 3,000 m and brain swelling ([HACE](g:hace)) is not seen below 4,000 m; both are emergencies that need descent and a doctor.

The main protection is a slow ascent. One review gives an average of 300 m per day of sleeping altitude above 2,000 m, and for a stay at 2,500–3,000 m, waiting 2 days before easing into training [[c:acc-ascent]]. Symptoms that get worse mean going down, not pushing on.

claims.text: Transient AMS (headache, anorexia, nausea) occurs in 10–30% of people at 2,500–3,000 m; pulmonary oedema is rare below 3,000 m and brain oedema is not seen below 4,000 m.

evidence.quote: Transient acute mountain sickness (headache, anorexia, and nausea) is present in 10-30% of subjects at altitudes between 2500 and 3000 m a.s.l.
Pulmonary edema is rarely seen below 3000 m a.s.l. and brain edema is not seen below 4000 m a.s.l.

claims.text: One review advises about 300 m per day of ascent above 2,000 m, and waiting 2 days at 2,500–3,000 m before gradually training.

evidence.quote: At higher altitudes, one should consider a staged ascent (average ascent rate 300 m/day above 2000 m a.s.l.), primarily in order to sleep and feel well, and minimize the risk of mountain sickness.
It is possible to travel to altitudes of 2500-3000 m a.s.l., wait for 2 days, and then gradually start to train.

steps.title: Days for a staged ascent
steps.problem: You sleep at 2,000 m and want to reach a sleeping altitude of 3,200 m. At an average of 300 m per day, how many days?
steps: Only the height gained above 2,000 m counts: 3,200 − 2,000 = 1,200 m.

points: Within minutes breathing and heart rate rise; EPO starts to climb within about 2 hours; plasma volume falls over 24–48 h, raising haemoglobin concentration with no new red cells.
Red cell mass needs weeks: about 9% more after 4 weeks at 2,500 m in one trial.
Concentration = Hb mass ÷ blood volume, so a rising concentration in the first days is a plasma effect, not more red cells.

Whether VO₂max at altitude comes back with acclimatisation is disputed: up about 8% from the day-1 low in 2 weeks at 2,340 m in one study, essentially none after long stays at higher altitude in a review.
AMS affects 10–30% at 2,500–3,000 m; ascend about 300 m per day above 2,000 m and go down if symptoms worsen.

variants.stem: An athlete flies to 2,500 m. Which change shows up first?

options.text: Breathing and heart rate rise within minutes
options.why: Correct: the ventilatory and heart-rate responses are the fast ones.

options.text: Red cell mass rises within a day
options.why: New red cells take days to appear and weeks to add up.
Haemoglobin mass takes weeks to rise; only plasma volume changes within 1–2 days.

variants.stem: About how soon after reaching a simulated 3,000 m did EPO start to rise?

options.why: Correct: significantly raised after 114 minutes.
Too slow: the signal starts within hours.
Confuses EPO with the red cell mass, which takes weeks.

options.text: Only once red cell mass had risen
options.why: Backwards: EPO is the signal that makes red cells.

variants.stem: A man has 700 g of haemoglobin in 5.0 L of blood (3.2 L plasma, 1.8 L red cells): 140 g·L⁻¹. After 3 days at 2,500 m his plasma volume is 10% lower and his haemoglobin mass is unchanged. What is his haemoglobin concentration now?

options.why: Raised the concentration by the same 10%: but plasma is only part of the blood, so blood volume falls less than 10%.
Divided by the new plasma volume alone, forgetting the red cells.
Assumed nothing changed: the haemoglobin is the same, but it now sits in less blood.

variants.stem: A man has 900 g of haemoglobin in 5.6 L of blood (3.4 L plasma, 2.2 L red cells): 161 g·L⁻¹. After 3 days at altitude his plasma volume is 8% lower and his haemoglobin mass is unchanged. What is his haemoglobin concentration now?

options.why: Raised the concentration by the same 8%: plasma is only part of the blood.
Divided by the new plasma volume alone, forgetting the red cells.
Assumed nothing changed: the same haemoglobin now sits in less blood.

variants.stem: A woman has 800 g of haemoglobin in 5.0 L of blood (3.0 L plasma, 2.0 L red cells): 160 g·L⁻¹. After 3 days at altitude her plasma volume is 12% lower and her haemoglobin mass is unchanged. What is her haemoglobin concentration now?

options.why: Raised the concentration by the same 12%: plasma is only part of the blood.
Divided by the new plasma volume alone, forgetting the red cells.
Assumed nothing changed: the same haemoglobin now sits in less blood.

variants.stem: After 3 days at 2,500 m, a cyclist's haemoglobin concentration is 6% higher than at home. What is the most likely reading?

options.text: Her plasma volume fell; haemoglobin mass has probably not changed yet
options.why: Correct: concentration rises when plasma shrinks, within 1–2 days.

options.text: She has made 6% more red cells in 3 days
options.why: Red cell mass needs weeks; EPO only started the process.

options.text: Her SaO₂ is back to sea-level values, so she is fully acclimatised
options.why: A higher concentration offsets some of the loss, but SaO₂ is still low and the slower changes are still to come.

variants.stem: You will race at 2,340 m. In one study VO₂max rose about 8% above its day-1 value within 14 days there; a review says peak VO₂ at altitude is essentially unchanged after long stays. What do you check first?

options.text: Which source is newer, since newer evidence always wins
options.why: Date alone does not decide: design, altitude and athletes do.

options.text: The altitude, stay length and athletes each statement covers
options.why: Correct: the review speaks of higher altitudes and long stays; the study of 8 elite cyclists at 2,340 m.

options.text: Nothing: a review always overrules one study
options.why: A review summarises, but may not cover your altitude; a small study can still fit your case better.

variants.stem: At 2,500–3,000 m, about what share of people get transient acute mountain sickness?

options.why: Far too low: it is common.
Correct, per a review of altitude adaptation.
Too high for these moderate altitudes.
Most people at moderate altitude do not get it.

variants.stem: A runner reaches a camp at 2,600 m. That night she has a headache and nausea. Her plan for tomorrow is a hard interval session. What is the better plan?

options.text: Rest or train easy at this height; go down if it worsens
options.why: Correct: mild AMS is usually temporary; worsening symptoms mean descent.

options.text: Do the intervals: sweating it out speeds up acclimatisation
options.why: Hard exercise on top of AMS does not clear it and can make it worse.

options.text: Move up 500 m to sleep so the body adapts faster
options.why: Going higher with symptoms raises the risk; ascent should be staged.

variants.stem: You sleep at 2,000 m and want to sleep at 3,500 m. At an average of 300 m per day above 2,000 m, how many days of ascent?

options.why: Divided the whole altitude (3,500 ÷ 300), not the height gained above 2,000 m.
Mixed up with the 'wait 2 days' advice after arrival.
Used 200 m per day by mistake (1,500 ÷ 200 = 7.5, so 8).

variants.solution: Height gained above 2,000 m = 1,500 m. 1,500 ÷ 300 = 5 days.

variants.stem: You sleep at 2,000 m and want to sleep at 3,200 m. At an average of 300 m per day above 2,000 m, how many days of ascent?

options.why: Divided the whole altitude (3,200 ÷ 300), not the height gained.
Mixed up with the 'wait 2 days' advice after arrival.
Used 200 m per day by mistake.

variants.stem: You sleep at 2,500 m and want to sleep at 3,400 m. At an average of 300 m per day above 2,000 m, how many days of ascent?

options.why: Divided the whole altitude (3,400 ÷ 300), not the height gained.
Mixed up with the 'wait 2 days' advice after arrival.
